tier_reason: The README table (CRC++ 2050/2200 ms, boost 2250/2000 ms, pycrc 2050/2240 ms, mhash 2250/2400 ms for 100 million iterations on x64/x86) matches the record exactly, but it is first-party with no CPU, compiler, flags, input size or CRC variant, and the repo holds no timing code (test/src contains only main.cpp, a unit test with no clock or timing calls), so it is C.
notes: Record is accurate: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE checked), 414 stars, 104 forks, not archived or a fork, last commit 2026-09-03 (active). Shortcomings: unreproducible first-party table with no methodology or benchmark code; win is only about 1.10x over boost and mhash on x64 (derived from page data), a tie with pycrc, and boost is about 1.10x faster on x86; no comparison with SIMD/PCLMUL or hardware CRC32 implementations. A WebSearch found no independent CRC++ vs boost::crc measurement.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to B: the SMHasher3 results summary (a well-known independent suite run by its maintainer, not the Rain author) lists rainbow-128 at 62.06 avg cycles on short keys against HighwayHash-128 at 99.09 and FarmHash-128.CM.seed1 at 69.61, and rainbow-256 at 103.65 against HighwayHash-256 at 154.48; raw/rainbow-128.txt confirms 62.06 cycles and 1.27-1.28 bytes/cycle. Not A because neither the summary nor the raw file names the CPU model, compiler or flags (only a nominal '@ 3.5 ghz' conversion); same treatment as the earlier SMHasher3-based B entries (ChibiHash, a5hash, MeowHash, AquaHash).

corrections.caveats: The README headline claim (fastest 128-bit and 256-bit non-crypto hash) is not supported by the SMHasher3 results page it links: several passing 128-bit hashes (a5hash-128, MuseAir-128, MeowHash) are faster in bulk and on short keys, and at 256 bits HighwayHash-256 and CityHashCrc-256 (which fails some tests) are faster in bulk. The only wins found are narrow (short-key latency against HighwayHash and FarmHash; MeowHash ties). Against the usual non-crypto incumbents it is slower on the same page: 64-bit rainbow is 61.63 cycles and 1.28 bytes/cycle vs XXH-64 52.60 and 3.99, and XXH3-128 (fails some tests) is 36.13 and 12.72. SMHasher3 results list the CPU nowhere; the SMHasher3 README describes the maintainer's machine (AMD Ryzen 9 3950X pinned to 3500 MHz, gcc 9.3) only for its runtime-comparison table, which fits the '@ 3.5 ghz' conversion but is not stated as the results machine. Results come from SMHasher3 20251015, 20251112 or 20260827 release builds. The table is the maintainer's single run; Rain's README licence line credits the SMHasher3 maintainer with improvements to the code, so the suite is not fully arm's length. Results were measured on Rainbow v3.7.1; the 4.0.0 release changed only Rainstorm (README: Rainbow digests unchanged). The repo's own results/smhasher3/rainbow-256-v3.7.1.txt came back as an empty file through raw.githubusercontent.com and was not used. The assigned URL github.com/DOSAYGO-Research/rain resolves to DOSAYGO-STUDIO/rain.

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup all match the SMHasher3 results summary and raw/rainbow-128.txt (whose small-key test is [1, 31]-byte keys although the summary header says 1-32). Metadata confirmed: Apache-2.0, 134 stars, 9 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-15 (active). Shortcomings: README 'fastest 128-bit and 256-bit hash' claim is false on the page it cites; wins only on short-key latency vs HighwayHash-128/256 and FarmHash-128.CM, about 2x slower in bulk than both, and slower than XXH-64 and XXH3 on both metrics; suite maintainer is credited with Rain code improvements.

tier_reason: The CVS snapshot's BENCHMARKS,v revision 1.17 (2003-01-28), reconstructed from the RCS file, holds the BeeCrypt-vs-Java modular exponentiation table and every number and quote in claimed_speedup matches it; it is first-party, gives compilers and machines but no flags, and the Java timing harness is not in the tree, so it is C.

corrections.workload: Modular exponentiation (1024-bit base ^ 1024-bit exponent mod 1024-bit modulus), 100 repetitions, wall time in seconds (less is better), BeeCrypt 2.0.0 to 2.3.0 (C with assembler) versus several Java VMs on 1999 to 2002 era machines (BENCHMARKS revision 1.17 and earlier).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler named per row (Visual C 6.0, Visual Studio .NET, gcc-2.95.x, gcc 3.2.1, Compaq C 6.3, Forte C 6.0 / Forte C++ 6.1); optimization flags not stated in this revision. The table predates tests/benchme.c (first revision 2003-03-01; BENCHMARKS revision 1.18 says 'Replaced with new benchmarking program results'); the C timings of that era come from beetest.c (now Attic/beetest.c,v, a loop of 100 mp32bnpowmod calls timed with clock()). The Java benchmark program is not in the CVS tree.
corrections.hardware: Per row, 1999 to 2002 era: Pentium III 450/600/800/1000, PIII Mobile 850, Pentium Pro 200, Athlon 1000/1200, Pentium 4M 1700, Alpha EV6.7 667, UltraSparc I 143 and II 450, PowerPC 604 166/604ev 375/G3 400/7450, Itanium 666/733, StrongARM 110, IBM zSeries 633, Sparc v8 70; Java rows (Pentium III 450/600, Pentium II 333, Pentium Pro 200, PowerPC G3/G4, UltraSparc I 143) were mostly measured on different machines, only a few coincide with BeeCrypt rows
corrections.caveats: The only numeric comparison reachable is against Java on 1999 to 2003 era hardware and JVMs (the table was removed from BENCHMARKS in revision 1.18, 2003-05-20; the newest revision 1.35 of 2015-12-28 holds only BeeCrypt-alone numbers, e.g. modular exponentiation score 64747 on a Core i7-2600). It says nothing about OpenSSL, libsodium or BoringSSL, so it is far off the usual incumbents and baseline_in_list is false. Java and BeeCrypt rows are mostly on different machines; the ratios quoted above use rows where machine and OS match as closely as the file allows. The C timings came from the old beetest.c program, not tests/benchme.c, and the Java harness is not public, so the comparison cannot be reproduced. The 5x-over-a-commercial-product remark names no product. An independent 2008 panthema.net speedtest (OpenSSL vs BeeCrypt vs Crypto++ vs Botan) exists but the host is EGRESS_BLOCKED here and search summaries gave conflicting AES numbers, so none of it is used. The benchmark page URL is a CVS snapshot zip; the data is in beecrypt/beecrypt/BENCHMARKS,v (revision 1.17 of 2003-01-28 and earlier). Source headers say LGPL 2.1 or later; the SourceForge project page lists LGPLv2. Unmaintained: last CVS change 2015-12-28, last file release 4.2.1 (SourceForge 'last update' 2013-04-23).

notes: Numbers verified by rebuilding BENCHMARKS revision 1.17 from the RCS file in the CVS snapshot: PIII 600/Win2000 4.3 vs 10.2 and 19.7 sec, PIII 450/Solaris 8 5.9 vs 17.1 sec, UltraSparc I 143/Solaris 8 40.7 vs 83.4 sec, and the 'twice to four times faster' quote all match. Shortcomings: baseline is 1999-2002 Java BigInteger, not OpenSSL or any C/C++ incumbent; first-party, flags unstated, Java harness not public, most Java and BeeCrypt rows on different machines; abandoned since 2015. Licence LGPL-2.1-or-later per source headers (SourceForge page says LGPLv2); 161 weekly downloads and 2 reviews (5.0) confirmed.
